newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Solana in Moscow for tough talks on NATO expansion.
newsitem.headline: Solana in Moscow for tough talks on NATO expansion.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana arrived in Moscow on Sunday to try to ease Russia's fears over the alliance's plans to take in new members from eastern and central Europe.
NATO officials said Solana was carrying proposals intended to soften the blow of the planned expansion, including a promise of a permanent consultative forum between the Cold War foes.

He is due to have five hours of talks on Monday with Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov. But opposition to NATO's plans is one of the few issues uniting Russians across the political spectrum and hopes of an early breakthrough are slim.
"All the questions for Russia and NATO will not be solved at a single meeting, even a five-hour one," Interfax news agency quoted a senior foreign ministry official as saying.
A government foreign policy expert said Russian officials were concerned that little might emerge from Solana's visit.

"We are slightly worried that Solana will come here as an American evangelist rather than as a negotiating partner," he said. "We are looking for a deal which would guarantee our national interests rather than verbal assurances that everyone is Moscow's friend."
As a measure of the sensitivity of the visit, reporters were kept at a distance when Solana flew in, the venue of Monday's talks were not announced and no media access was expected.
Russian officials have frequently condemned NATO's plans to expand eastwards, which they say would threaten Russia's security and open new divisions in Europe.
NATO is expected to issue formal invitations to the first new members at a summit in Madrid in July. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are expected to be first in the queue.
"If NATO wants to expand let it expand, but we are against this," Defence Minister Igor Rodionov said last week.
Asked if he saw NATO's expansion as a danger to Russia, he said: "Russia faces potential threats from the west, south and east...But these are potential threats, not enemies."

President Boris Yeltsin also opposes the expansion plans. But a bout of pneumonia has put him in hospital for more than a week, thwarting his attempts to make an energetic return to the Kremlin after heart surgery and raising questions about his ability to see out his four-year term of office.
Solana, asked by the alliance to negotiate a treaty or a charter with Moscow, was expected to meet Primakov at a government residence outside the capital.
"We do not plan to invite the press to the talks in order to give both sides the chance of working as effectively as possible," a foreign ministry official told Interfax.
NATO has already said it will not station nuclear weapons on the territory of the first new members and hinted it will make the same commitment for conventional forces.
Independent Russian analysts say Moscow is keen to win as many concessions as possible before NATO enlargement goes ahead and that it has toughened its rhetoric in the last few weeks.
Primakov urged NATO earlier this month to speed up efforts to forge a special relationship with Russia.

He said Moscow wanted the right to joint decision-making on issues which concern its "vital interests" and revisions of the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty, which limits the number of conventional arms on the continent and where they can be placed.
